source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Compare CMS and G1 mechanisms and explain scenario selection, covering the six frozen repository variants without expanding into a separate CMS-only or G1-only answer contract.

sources.title: Oracle Java 8 HotSpot VM GC Tuning Guide — Concurrent Mark Sweep (CMS) Collector
anchors: CMS pauses application threads at the start and again near the middle of a major collection, while most tracing and sweeping run concurrently with the application.
Concurrent mode failure occurs when CMS cannot finish before the tenured generation fills or available free blocks cannot satisfy an allocation.
CMS concurrent tracing can leave floating garbage for a later cycle and concurrent GC threads consume processor resources that would otherwise be available to the application.

sources.title: Oracle Java 8 HotSpot VM GC Tuning Guide — Garbage-First Garbage Collector
anchors: G1 uses a pause prediction model and selects how many regions to collect based on the pause target.
G1 evacuates live objects from selected regions, thereby compacting and freeing memory; Oracle explicitly contrasts this with CMS not doing compaction.
G1 is not a real-time collector and meeting the pause target is probabilistic, not an absolute guarantee.

sources.title: Oracle Java 8 HotSpot VM GC Tuning Guide — Garbage-First Garbage Collector Tuning
anchors: G1 uses Region remembered sets and write barriers so selected regions can be collected without scanning the entire heap.
Young and mixed collections include stop-the-world evacuation pauses.
G1 uses SATB for concurrent marking and remembered-set maintenance has CPU/memory work.

sources.title: Oracle Java 25 GC Tuning Guide — Garbage-First Garbage Collector Tuning
anchors: Remembered-set merge/scan work can be significant, and region size trades fewer cross-region references against more live data to evacuate.
Concurrent remembered-set refinement can consume substantial CPU; shifting that work into pauses trades throughput against latency.
MaxGCPauseMillis participates in the latency/throughput balance rather than providing a hard SLA.

sources.title: Oracle JDK 9 GC Tuning Guide — Available Collectors
anchors: CMS is described as a shorter-pause collector that shares processor resources with the application.
CMS is deprecated as of JDK 9.

sources.title: Oracle JDK Migration Guide — Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector
anchors: G1 is the default garbage collector in JDK 9 and later releases.

sources.title: Oracle JDK 24 Migration Guide — Removed Tools and Components
anchors: The Concurrent Mark Sweep garbage collector was removed in JDK 14.

claims.text: CMS performs most old-generation tracing and sweeping concurrently with the application but still has stop-the-world initial-mark and remark pauses and consumes application-visible CPU during concurrent phases.

Because CMS does not normally compact and must finish before old-generation space becomes unusable, its comparison should include fragmentation/free-block sensitivity, floating garbage, and concurrent mode failure rather than presenting concurrency as cost-free.
G1 partitions the heap into regions, uses marking information to select collection sets, and evacuates live objects from selected regions so reclamation also compacts memory.
G1 uses a history-based pause prediction model to size collection work against a soft pause target; young/mixed evacuation is stop-the-world and the target is not an absolute real-time guarantee.
Region-local collection depends on remembered sets and barriers for cross-region references, and remembered-set refinement/scan work can trade CPU, memory and pause time.

G1 became the default collector in JDK 9 and later; CMS was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 14, so modern selection advice must be version-aware and not treat CMS as a current JDK 14+ deployment option.

writer_constraints: Cover all six frozen CMS-versus-G1 source variants, including the scenario-selection variant.
Keep the answer comparative: do not duplicate the adjacent CMS-only execution-flow or G1-only mechanism Canonicals beyond the detail needed to explain the comparison.
Do not say CMS is pause-free; preserve initial-mark and remark stop-the-world boundaries.
Do not say G1 is pause-free or real-time; preserve stop-the-world evacuation and the soft/probabilistic pause target.
Explain Region, Collection Set, evacuation and remembered-set mechanics rather than only naming algorithms.
Include CMS concurrent-mode failure, floating-garbage/CPU tradeoffs, and non-compaction as relevant historical boundaries.
Include JDK lifecycle facts: G1 default from JDK 9+, CMS deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 14.
Do not fabricate production workload, pause, CPU, throughput or migration results; scenario advice must specify what to measure instead.
Do not claim G1 is universally faster or always lower-pause; recommend same-workload validation for historical JDK 8 migration decisions.
